This paper introduces a novel, resource-efficient verification method for the majority of circuits, relying on the application of a single qubit by a user. We developed a new convolutional neural network (CNN) model that mimics the behavior of hypercomplex cells by taking the outputs of a standard V1-like CNN and applying end-stopping mechanisms to its complex cell units. Holes (MBHs) in local star-forming galaxies has highlighted a discrepancy between MBH masses and the stellar mass of their host galaxies, known as the $M_{\rm BH}-M_{\rm host}$ relation. This study investigates whether the evolution of star formation in galaxies influences the establishment of this relation. We utilize the IllustrisTNG cosmological simulation to examine the star formation histories of galaxies hosting MBHs with masses around $10^9 M_\odot$ at redshifts $z=0$ and $z=0.5$. We find that the specific star formation rates (sSFR) of these host galaxies decline over time, yet the decline is significantly slower for hosts of $10^9 M_\odot$ black holes compared to those with $10^7 M_\odot$ black holes. This difference is attributed to the fact that hosts of $10^9 M_\odot$ black holes are typically more massive and reside in larger halos, resulting in lower sSFRs even at high redshifts. Consequently, the distinct star formation evolution between host populations drives the observed separation in the $M_{\rm BH}-M_{\rm host}$ relation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the IllustrisTNG simulation successfully reproduces the specific star formation rate distributions of observed galaxies, validating its capability to model the star formation evolution of MBH hosts.

This paper introduces a novel approach to generate explanations for classification models by leveraging the concept of "contrastive sets." A contrastive set comprises all data points that share the same classification label as a specific target instance, excluding the target itself. We demonstrate that constructing these sets enables the creation of meaningful explanations through the derivation of "explanation functions." These functions utilize contrasts to quantify how much an arbitrary data point resembles the target, thereby highlighting its most similar counterparts within the same class. We further show that these explanation functions can be formulated as a specific type of autoencoder, facilitating their efficient computation. Finally, we present empirical results confirming that explanations generated via contrast sets are both semantically meaningful and capable of supporting effective few-shot learning.

A family of vectors $\mathcal{T} = \{T_1, \dots, T_m\}$, where each $T_i \in \{0, 1\}^n$, is termed a *separating system* for $\mathcal{S}$ if, for every pair of distinct sets $S_i$ and $S_j$, there exists at least one coordinate $k$ where $T_i[k] \neq T_j[k]$. This concept generalizes the well-known notion of a *superimposed code* (or separated code). In superimposed coding, the codeword for any element $S_i$ must evaluate to 1 on all positions corresponding to elements within $S_i$, and 0 elsewhere. Consequently, the codeword for the empty set is entirely zero, and the codeword for the full set $\{1, \dots, n\}$ is entirely one. While superimposed codes are typically studied with a fixed universe size $n$, this work focuses on the more general case where $n$ is unbounded. We establish that the minimum length of a separating system for a given set family $\mathcal{S}$ is exactly equal to the dimension of the linear span of the characteristic vectors of those sets.
